executive_summary: This collection window (June 1-7, 2027) is the fiftieth archived window. Two signals cleared the cross-source corroboration bar this window, both carrying forward from the ongoing spring/summer runway cycle rather than originating in this window specifically: a beaded-jewelry accessory revival (multi-outlet editorial convergence citing Celine, Chanel, and Polo Ralph Lauren runway styling) and a sleepwear-as-outerwear/relaxed-tailoring menswear shift (editorial convergence citing Milan menswear runway presentations). Met Gala 2027 was checked a sixth consecutive window -- still no theme, co-chair, or red-carpet coverage of any kind has surfaced. Consistent with the prior window's corrected framing, this is logged as a standing, unresolved coverage gap for an event that occurred May 3, 2027, not a calendar question -- the index's tracking window has been past the event date for five prior windows with no coverage appearing. Wales Bonner/Hermes and the CFDA Fashion Fund/Awards questions were not re-litigated this window per SKILL.md workflow note 10; no new coverage surfaced for either.

top_signals.name: Beaded jewelry and accessory revival
top_signals.evidence: Multiple editorial outlets (Marie Claire, Who What Wear, Fashionista, L'Officiel USA) independently reported a beaded-jewelry accessory wave for spring/summer, each citing overlapping runway reference points: stacked colorful beaded necklaces and beaded earrings at Celine under Michael Rider, draped beaded necklaces layered over looks at Chanel, and full-wrist beaded bracelet stacks at Polo Ralph Lauren. Coverage extends past necklaces into beaded bags, footwear, and paillette embellishment. Framed by more than one outlet as a nostalgic, tactile counter-move against 'quiet luxury' minimalism.
top_signals.index_note: Editorial-sector convergence on a shared descriptive frame (beaded accessories, named across four independent outlets, tied to three named runway houses) -- treated as editorial_amplified rather than designer_originated since the trend claim is the outlets' synthesis across multiple houses' collections, not a single designer's stated intent.
top_signals.human_editor_note: derive_confidence() would land this at 'high' (corroboration_count 4, two distinct source_sectors). Holding at 'medium' by manual override: three of the four corroborating outlets (Marie Claire, Who What Wear, Fashionista) are enthusiast/service-jewelry verticals within the same outlets that also run shopping-recommendation content, which raises the risk that 'trend' coverage here is partly commerce-driven framing rather than independent editorial judgment converging by coincidence. That's a source-incentive concern this index's own voice rules flag (no shopping-recommendation logic gets laundered into a confidence score), not a corroboration-count problem, so it's a manual downgrade rather than a taxonomy gap.

top_signals.name: Sleepwear-as-outerwear / relaxed menswear tailoring
top_signals.evidence: WWD, Wallpaper*, and other editorial coverage of the spring/summer menswear runway cycle independently described a shift toward fluid silhouettes, lightweight layering, and pajama-inspired dressing -- striped sleep sets, negligee-like tops, and silk robe styling worn as outerwear at Milan menswear presentations -- alongside looser, deconstructed tailoring replacing rigid suiting. Thom Browne's Milan menswear show (technical-nylon seersucker, garden-party staging) was cited by multiple outlets as the season's clearest single expression of the lighter, breathable-fabric direction.
top_signals.index_note: Editorial convergence across independent outlets on the same seasonal silhouette description (relaxed tailoring plus sleepwear-coded pieces), anchored to specific named runway presentations rather than a single brand's marketing claim -- editorial_amplified, not designer_originated.
top_signals.human_editor_note: Not upgraded to 'high' despite 3 sources across 2 sectors: the runway sector citation here is really editorial outlets describing runway shows secondhand (WWD's own runway review counts as editorial reportage, not an independent designer-origin statement), so the cross-sector diversity is thinner in practice than the raw tag count implies. 'Medium' reflects strong same-sector convergence rather than genuinely independent cross-sector confirmation.
